hook.spoken: Today we're talking about hooks. If you want your videos to perform better, you need to focus on leveling up your hooks. Now look, I've studied literally thousands of videos and it turns out if your hooks are not working, there's only four mistakes you could be making.

(mistake 1: delay) topic arrives too late; cut the fluff lines so the topic lands in the first 1-2 s ('craziest thing I've ever seen' gives zero context); retention falls off a cliff in the first 2 s
(mistake 2: confusion) fewer, simpler words at a 6th-grade level, active voice; test: can the hook be read two ways? Rewrite until it can't

(mistake 3: irrelevance) say you/your, not I/me; frame around a known need-to-have pain ('If you struggle with acne, try these 3 things' beats 'three skincare trends')

insights: A hook has one job: get the right viewer to opt in. It needs two things: topic clarity and on-target curiosity.
Mistake 1, delay: the topic must land in the first 1-2 s; cut the fluff lines above it. Vague 'you won't believe this' hooks give zero context.
Mistake 2, confusion: fewer and simpler words (6th-grade level), active voice; if the hook can be read two ways, rewrite it.
Mistake 3, irrelevance: say you/your, not I/me, and frame a need-to-have pain, not a nice-to-know topic.

Mistake 4, disinterest: create contrast, A (what they believe or do now) vs B (your alternative that solves the pain faster, better or cheaper). Stated contrast names both; implied contrast names only B.
A hook is usually 2-3 lines: clarity in line 1, contrast in lines 2-3.
why_it_works: A named diagnostic ('four horsemen': delay, confusion, irrelevance, disinterest) turns a vague skill into a checklist.
Every mistake gets a bad and a fixed example side by side.
The contrast idea explains why contrarian hooks work (it re-agitates the viewer's unsolved pain).

note: User wants her hooks, fonts and narration pattern; huge Shorts creator (4.5K Shorts), study by views not 1-by-1
hook_bank: I'm building a secret room with $0. (185M; I'm-doing-X + tiny budget)
I'm surprising my family with their favorite lost things, but they don't know I've been stealing their stuff for the past year. (87M; dramatic irony)
Can you cook faster than fast food? (107M; can-you race, answered in the last line)
How many flavors can you get with a dollar? That's going to be like $20. (77M; how-many + stake in line 2)
What drink can I get for a dollar? (76M; what-does-$1-get-you)
I love strawberries, but every time I buy them they disappear the next day. (72M; mystery with suspects, twist: 'the thief was me')
My grandma thinks Christmas is expensive, so I'm gonna prove her wrong… with five dollars. (72M; someone's belief -> prove it wrong)
Tada. How do you do that? (65M; result first, ends on the countdown to it = seamless loop)
One dollar boba. My grandma spends way too much on boba. (59M; say the title as a label, then the stake)
You can find golden dirt. This is a $25 bag of dirt. (51M; surprising claim + exact price)
My mom thinks this food is from a famous chef. But what she doesn't know is it's $1 spaghetti. (40M; secret the viewer shares)
If you cut a cucumber in half and rub it against itself, it produces this bitter foam. (37M, posted twice; if-you hack)
Is the 5-second rule real? Because I'm testing it to save you from food poisoning. (30M; question + 'because… for you')
insights: Channel: 4,579 Shorts, 12.4M followers. 79 of her 100 biggest non-sponsored hits come from her first ~460 Shorts (Jul 2022 - Nov 2025, median 1.5M views). Since Nov 2025 she has posted ~4,100 more (~13 a day) at a median of 155-460K: volume did not replace the scripted story.

Narration numbers (top 80 by views): talking on frame 1 (median 0.04 s), ~11 words in the first 3 s, ~3.6 words/s, 0.8 pauses per 10 s (every breath cut), stories ~39 s / ~140 words, and 91% end while she is still talking (median 0.33 s of silence at the end).

The hook is the title said out loud: 43 of 61 narrated hits say at least half the title's key words in the first 3 s. Hook types in the top 80: question (21: 'Can you…', 'How many…', 'What does $1 get you…', 'Is X real?'), 'I'm doing X with $0 / $1' (18), a label ('One dollar boba.'), 'If you…' hacks, 'My mom thinks… but what she doesn't know…'.

Story engine: line 2 gives a character and a stake (a belief, a price, a budget: 'my grandma spends way too much on boba'); then a plan ('so I'm gonna…', 'let's get boba-ing'); then steps chained with so (49/61 scripts), but (47/61), then, now; obstacles ('but my secret room has a big problem'); a re-hook question late in the video ('but is it better than her favorite café? Let's find out', 11/61, at a median 71% through); the answer is the last words.

Endings: the payoff or twist is the final line with no outro or CTA ('for a dollar I got water', 'the thief was me', '$248. No ice cream for you', 'it weighs nothing'). Reveal-first videos start on the finished result ('Tada.') and end on the countdown to it ('3, 2…'), so the loop is seamless.

Exact numbers as proof and punchline: 3.3 numbers per 100 words ('81 cents', '1.87', '$265.86'); a number in the first 3 s of 32% of hooks. Titles: 29% questions, 25% with $, 10% 'vs', median 6 words.

On-screen text is the native editor look, not motion design: TikTok Sans-style SemiBold (the old TikTok/CapCut font), lowercase, white with a thick black outline, 1-4 words at the vertical centre (~50-57%); another speaker's words in yellow under a small 'my mom:' label; the catchphrase as a big stacked title ('let's get boba-ing'); a cyan-outlined dark pill for running tallies and prices (flavours ': 4', '$2.40', '$1.07'); an emoji checklist with checkmarks at the top as ingredients get added; red hand-drawn arrows on the key object. From 2025 the captions got smaller and lighter.

Covers and first frames: the whole premise in one picture (chef hat + burger at the McDonald's drive-thru; the finished watermelon; a face + the object); the first frame is mid-action (pickaxe already in the wall).

Cast and running gag: mom, grandma and dad are the sceptics to prove wrong; 'all this for one subscriber' (7/61) works as a subscribe CTA inside the story. A sponsor (Creator Now) is written in as a plot step, not a break (26M).
Reposting winners works: Cucumber Hack got 37M twice (Sept 2025 and Jan 2026), What's Faster 107M then 35M, the $1 ice cream 77M then 20M.
Her biggest Shorts since late 2025 are 6-17 s engagement-bait clips ('SUBSCRIBE! U MAY NOT SEE ME AGAIN', 53M; 'COMMENT FOR 7 YEARS OF GOOD LUCK', 55M): not a brand tactic.
why_it_works: Title, first spoken line and premise are one sentence, so the viewer knows the game in 1-2 s and stays for the answer: the hook is a question the last line must answer.
Constant forward motion: every sentence is a new step (so / but / then), ~3.6 words/s, no pauses, so there is no moment to swipe.
Tiny, concrete stakes ($0, $1, five dollars) and exact numbers make it feel real and measurable.
The late re-hook question ('but is it better? let's find out') resets curiosity just before the payoff.
Ending on the payoff with no outro makes the loop instant (replays count as views on Shorts).
A sceptical family member gives emotion and someone to prove wrong.

gaps: speaker-coloured captions: a second voice (tracks) in yellow under a small 'my mom:' label
outlined / glowing border on text boxes (her cyan tally pill around a counter)

steal: Question-race hooks proven on screen: 'What's faster: A or B?' with two timers; 'Can you find X in 10 seconds?'; 'How many taps to X?' with a tally.
Hook text = title = the first VO line, spoken from 0.0 s.
Script as a chain: stake line -> 'so we...' -> 'but...' -> 'so...', ~3.5-4 words/s, no pauses (max_pause 0.35).
A re-hook question at ~70%, right before the proof.
End on the payoff words, no outro, so the video loops back into the question.
Exact numbers everywhere: '3 minutes 47 seconds vs 12 seconds', '4 taps'.
Faceless version of her on-camera sceptic: a text-message sceptic.
Cover = the premise in one image; repost a best video after ~3 months with a new hook.
lessons: The hook is the title said out loud; the last line answers it
Talk from frame 1 at ~3.6 words/s and end on the payoff (91% end mid-speech)
Creator-native text: lowercase white with a thick outline, 1-4 words
Repost winners months later with a new hook; volume doesn't replace a scripted story

@JennyHoyos is an 18-year-old YouTuber who is absolutely crushing Shorts. She’s done over 600 million views in the past year alone, ave

note: Same creator (Jenny Hoyos) explaining her approach in an interview; learn from it too
insights: Context (Oct 2023): she was 18, averaging ~10M views per Short, 600M views in a year. Mindset: 'I don't ask if it'll go viral; I can figure out how to make it viral.' Anything can go viral with a story and a twist.
Investment = a personal why + irony, the creator as the hero: 'my kitchen is broken, so to fix it I have to cook to make money'.
Visual first: she sketches the first frame on an iPad like a long-form thumbnail before writing any words. Test: the hook would work as a long-form title + thumbnail, and makes sense without sound.

Series framing: in the $1 fast-food series the first frame shows the restaurant (more people know the brand than her face), the item in front and '$1 burrito' dead centre, always the same layout, so viewers recognise it and binge the playlist.

Readability: scripts at 5th grade or under (readabilityformulas.com); MrBeast's Shorts score ~1st grade. She says what 'profit' means instead of the word ('business', 'finance' push the grade up). Test audience: her 7- and 10-year-old nieces who barely speak English.
Hook writing: 'what would it sound like if [big creator] made this?' for each of ~10 big creators, pick favourites, compare viewed-vs-swiped, then add her own twist ('steal like an artist').

Structure: hook + a spoken foreshadow of the ending (two lines, 3 s or less: 'I'm going to the beach… and I'm going to surprise someone with $100 at the end'); then a transition that keeps the pace ('so I cooked it illegally', not 'let's get started', which breaks pace); then but / therefore storytelling; the promised end arrives with a twist (mom dropped the $5 gift: 'you're the best daughter' / 'I'm your only one').
Process: idea -> hook -> the last line (written before filming, with a blank for the reaction) -> foreshadow -> rough script or bullets -> film -> revise the script -> edit.

Mechanism = visible progress toward a known end (MrBeast's closing circle; 'there are 3 things we need' with the list on screen). Her explanation of her virality: viewers have a clear expectation of what they'll see and what's at the end.
Every second counts: a Short lost 25% of viewers in its last second; trimming that 1 s took retention from 83% to 88% and it took off. On a 30 s Short, 1 s is ~3% of retention.

Benchmarks (her channel, 2023): viewed-vs-swiped averages ~70% on Shorts, hers 85%; average retention 95% (rewatches); 90%+ is her floor to blow up; her best length is exactly 34 s; under 30 s a Short needs over 100% retention.

Platforms want different cuts: the same video got 1M on TikTok and 1K on Shorts, later the reverse. Shorts: slower, more story, ~34 s. TikTok (then): 10-20 s, dense, scrollable, few jokes. Reels: more mature, often muted, so very visual with subtitles every second, built to share.

Ideas: 1,000 in a Google Doc, ~10 get made. The best come from real life (grandma got free detergent by complaining; a $20 ratatouille -> 'infinite ratatouille' garden, 30M). Filter: do I want to make it, is it possible, is the hook good, is the mechanism good, will people rewatch, where's the virality; her editor-strategist narrows 25 to 10 by 'simple yet complex'.

Hunches: shares matter (a Short with a 20% share-to-view rate had 92% viewed-vs-swiped); retention matters less than people think (a Short at 70% retention on its first 100K views still reached 10M on returning viewers): 'it's viewer satisfaction'. Early on she posted daily and read every retention graph ('quantity makes quality').
why_it_works: It turns her channel's patterns (question hooks, payoff-last endings, story chains) into a repeatable recipe with numbers behind each step.
The expectation-then-twist rule explains both the retention (people wait for the promised end) and the loop (the twist lands on the last frame).
Designing for a child who barely speaks English forces the visual, simple hook that also works muted and across languages.

gaps: script check in ./vtk validate: reading grade (5th or under) and a foreshadow line in the first 3 s

insights: The format: set up an obvious expectation (the caption says a plane is flying dangerously low; the person looks up), and just before it should arrive, a paper plane sails in carrying the message. The setup alone makes people wait; no story needed. Original 24.5M views, a second version 6.4M ('You're a really good Mom').

The sound does half the work: both versions use the same real plane-flyover recording, which builds ~5-6 dB louder and brighter for ~5 s and peaks right as the paper plane crosses. The ear promises a jet getting closer, the eyes get a sheet of paper, and the roar keeps going over it: that mismatch is the joke. Without the sound it's just someone looking at the sky; the trend lives in the audio too (the same sound in both versions).
Businesses reused the exact setup with their own message and still went viral: a Toyota dealer ('Buy a Toyota'), a smoothie shop ('Fall Specials Out Now!'): 2.4M and 1.9M.
Their lesson: reuse proven formats and put the message at the moment attention peaks.
The breakdown itself is faceless: it opens on the viral example for 9 s with a view-count badge and no narration, then editorial kinetic type and rounded example cards on a dark teal gradient.
Comment-keyword CTA ('Comment "Formats" and we'll send it') pulled 868 comments on 3,392 likes, about one comment per four likes.
why_it_works: The audio builds the expectation: an approaching jet roar that swells for seconds makes everyone wait for the plane, then the picture breaks it at the sound's peak.
Anticipation does the retention: everyone waits for the plane, and the paper plane pays it off with a laugh.
The message lands at peak attention, so it's the most-watched frame of the video.
One location, a sheet of paper and a marker: cheap to copy, which is why brands could reuse it.

insights: Micro-fame = authority density per follower, not follower count: 50K followers who all see you as THE expert out-earn 2M general followers (40x more). Test: if you polled your followers 'who do you trust most in this niche?', would they say you? Followers who don't trust you dilute the audience (food colouring in water); bought followers or follower ads make it worse.

Why it's fast now, 3 algorithm shifts: zero-ramp virality (a brand-new account can hit 1M views on day 2), automatic targeting (the feed finds the right viewers within a couple of videos), unlimited scale (For You feeds show extra posts to non-followers, so ~10 posts a day don't fatigue followers).

His numbers: a new Instagram account 0 -> 60K followers in 90 days (~1,000/day), 5.5M views (>1% of viewers follow), 20K emails, $100K revenue. A client went 0 -> 100K followers in 12 months and owns the backpacking-review niche (1M+ view videos, brand deals, five-figure product launch).

Unique positioning angle: find white space on 7 attributes and stack them (they multiply): topic selection, substance depth, unique stories (can't be copied without lying), avatar specificity (e.g. social media for mortgage brokers), delivery style (tone, cadence, dress), storytelling format (challenges where everyone does listicles), visual format (cinematic where everyone is raw: it's the contrast with the field that wins). Open niche: one attribute is enough; crowded niche: stack several.

Transpositioning: don't clone the leader in your niche (they have a compounding head start); borrow what works in a distant niche. Copying a signature visual style mostly helps its owner; substance and delivery are the moat.
Hold back case studies and big social proof while small: '5,000 followers, and I grew someone to 100K' feels incongruent.

3-2-1 content mix (7 posts a week): 3 topic buckets x 2 videos + 1 'chaos agent' (a random test from another niche, or a triple-down). One bucket is broad (reach, a shot at virality, still builds authority); two are narrow (the buyer's pains and outcomes: fewer views, more trust and conversion per view). After 2 weeks, kill a bucket that flopped on all 4 videos and promote a new one (from the research or the chaos slot).

Choosing buckets: list 20-25 competitor channels with 25K-250K followers, take their last 3 months sorted by outlier score with engagement >= 2% (filters out paid brand deals), analyse the top 50-100 (topic, hook, format, structure) and chart which topic buckets win.
The talk sells his tools (a channel watch-list / outlier-analysis app, coaching); the frameworks work without them.
why_it_works: Reframes the goal from views to trust inside one niche, which changes what to post (narrow, useful) and what to measure.
Concrete, checkable frameworks (7 attributes, 3-2-1, the 2-week kill rule) with his own live numbers as proof.
steal: Plan each week 3-2-1: one broad bucket for reach, two narrow buckets for the buyer's pains, one chaos slot for tests; kill a bucket after 4 flops.
Pick a lane by stacking white space (topic, audience slice, format, visual style); check what the field looks like before choosing a look.
Borrow formats from distant niches instead of cloning the category leader.
Save social proof (user counts, case studies) until the numbers are congruent; prove it on screen instead.
Research competitors' outliers (last 3 months, engagement >= 2%) before choosing buckets.

gaps: Multi-channel watch list with an outlier score (views / the channel's median), last-3-months and engagement filters, and a topic-bucket chart (channel studies cover one channel at a time).
Content buckets on ideas + a per-bucket report from posted metrics (the 2-week kill rule).
